html:
Surah Al-Fātiḥah (The Opening) is the first surah of the Qur'an — seven verses that every Muslim recites in every rakʿah of every obligatory and voluntary prayer. Ibn Kathīr opens his tafsīr by listing the surah's names recorded in the Prophetic practice and the Companion-literature: al-Fātiḥah (The Opening), Umm al-Kitāb and Umm al-Qur'ān (Mother of the Book, Mother of the Qur'an), al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī (The Seven Oft-Repeated, per Al-Ḥijr 15:87), al-Ḥamd (The Praise), al-Ṣalāh (The Prayer — because its recitation is the prayer), al-Shifāʾ (The Cure), and al-Ruqyah (The Healing Incantation). The dominant opinion among the mufassirūn — Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, and the majority of the Ṣaḥābah via Ibn ʿAbbās — classifies Al-Fātiḥah as Makkī, revealed in the earliest Makkan period and establishing the formula of prayer before the detailed laws of worship came. A minority Madanī opinion exists, and a third view holds it was revealed twice — once in Makkah and once in Madinah — but al-Qurṭubī in al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qur'an considers the Makkī position decisive on the grounds that the five daily prayers were instituted before the Hijrah and prayer without Al-Fātiḥah is unattested in any early narration.

The surah's doctrinal weight rests on two foundational hadith, both in the Ṣaḥīḥayn and both beyond dispute. The first is the obligation hadith: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 756 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 394 record ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit — the Prophet ﷺ said, “There is no prayer for the one who does not recite the opening of the Book” (lā ṣalāta li-man lam yaqra' bi-Fātiḥati al-Kitāb). This hadith is the pillar for the Shāfiʿī and Ḥanbalī ruling that Al-Fātiḥah is obligatory on every worshipper in every rakʿah — imām, follower (ma'mūm), and worshipper praying alone (munfarid). The Ḥanafī school holds that the obligation falls on the imām and the one praying alone but not on the follower, grounding this in the general command to listen when the Qur'an is recited (Al-Aʿrāf 7:204). The Mālikī school distinguishes: obligatory in silent prayers, forgiven in audible prayers while the imām recites. The dispute is among the oldest in Islamic fiqh and runs on textual preference, not on the authenticity of the hadith — which is unanimously ṣaḥīḥ. The second foundational narration is the ḥadīth qudsī that divides the surah itself: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 395 records Abū Hurayrah — the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah has said, “I have divided the prayer (ṣalāh) between Me and My servant into two halves, and My servant shall have what he has asked for. When the servant says 'Al-ḥamdu li-llāhi Rabbi-l-ʿālamīn,' Allah says, 'My servant has praised Me.' When he says 'Ar-Raḥmāni-r-Raḥīm,' Allah says, 'My servant has extolled Me.' When he says 'Māliki yawmi-d-dīn,' Allah says, 'My servant has glorified Me — and once He said: My servant has entrusted himself to Me.' When he says 'Iyyāka naʿbudu wa iyyāka nastaʿīn,' Allah says, 'This is between Me and My servant — and My servant shall have what he has asked for.' When he says 'Ihdinā-ṣ-ṣirāṭa-l-mustaqīm…,' Allah says, 'This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he has asked for.'” The ḥadīth qudsī makes the structural reading of the surah literal: the first three verses are praise directed to Allah, the fifth verse is the pivot where worship and petition exchange hands, and the final verses are petition answered by Allah Himself.

The description of Al-Fātiḥah as al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī — the Seven Oft-Repeated — comes directly from the Qur'an: Al-Ḥijr 15:87 — wa-la-qad ātaynāka sabʿan min-al-mathānī wa-l-Qur'ān al-ʿaẓīm (“And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the great Qur'an”). Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4474, 4703 record Abū Hurayrah and Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā: the Prophet ﷺ said to Abū Saʿīd, “I will teach you a surah which is the greatest surah of the Qur'an before you leave the mosque,” then told him it is al-Ḥamdu li-llāhi Rabbi-l-ʿālamīn — the opening of Al-Fātiḥah — “and it is the Seven Oft-Repeated and the Great Qur'an that has been given to me.” Why seven verses, and why oft-repeated? Ibn Kathīr collects the Companion-glosses: oft-repeated because recited in every rakʿah of every prayer; oft-repeated because its meanings are inexhaustible and the believer returns to them again and again; oft-repeated because Allah divided it between Himself and His servant and both sides of that exchange recur in every ṣalāh. The verse-count brings up a famous madhhab dispute: does the Basmala (bismi-llāhi-r-Raḥmāni-r-Raḥīm) count as the first verse of Al-Fātiḥah or not? The Shāfiʿī school counts the Basmala as verse one and recites it audibly in audible prayers. The Ḥanafī and Ḥanbalī schools hold the Basmala is a verse of the Qur'an (revealed at the head of every surah except Al-Tawbah) but is not counted as part of Al-Fātiḥah's seven verses, and is recited silently. The Mālikī school holds the Basmala is not part of Al-Fātiḥah at all except in Surah Al-Naml 27:30, and omits it in prayer. All three positions produce seven verses — Shāfiʿī by including Basmala as v.1; Ḥanafī and Ḥanbalī by splitting ṣirāṭa-lladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim and ghayri-l-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-la-ḍ-ḍāllīn; Mālikī by starting the count at al-ḥamdu li-llāhi. Ibn Ḥajar in Fatḥ al-Bārī walks through all three with scrupulous fairness and declines to adjudicate — the dispute is grounded in the Mushaf transmission from the Ṣaḥābah and all three positions have ancient footing. The Qur'an the Muslim recites is identical in all three schools; only the counting convention differs.

Ibn Kathīr's structural reading of Al-Fātiḥah divides the surah into three movements that the ḥadīth qudsī (Muslim 395) ratifies explicitly. The first movement is praise — verses 1 to 4 (or 2 to 4 in the non-Basmala counting): al-ḥamdu li-llāhi Rabbi-l-ʿālamīn • ar-Raḥmāni-r-Raḥīm • Māliki yawmi-d-dīn. Al-Qurṭubī draws out the theological architecture: al-ḥamd (grateful praise) is distinct from al-shukr (gratitude for a benefit received) — al-ḥamd is praise for who Allah intrinsically is, independent of what He has done for me. The three divine titles that follow — Rabb (Lord, Nurturer), al-Raḥmān ar-Raḥīm (The Most Merciful, The Especially Merciful), and Mālik yawmi-d-dīn (Owner/King of the Day of Judgment) — map onto Ibn Taymiyyah's framework of divine action: Allah is Lord of creation (rubūbiyyah), Lord of mercy (which flows from rubūbiyyah), and Lord of accountability (which closes the circle). The second movement is the single pivot verse — verse 5 (or 4 in Mālikī counting): iyyāka naʿbudu wa iyyāka nastaʿīn (“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help”). Al-Qurṭubī notes the grammatical fronting of iyyāka (“You alone”) before the verb — classical Arabic uses this inversion specifically for exclusivity: not merely “we worship You” but “You and no other do we worship.” This is the pivot where praise turns into relationship: the servant has described Allah; now the servant addresses Allah. Ibn Kathīr marks this verse as the hinge of all tawḥīd al-ʿibādah (oneness in worship) in the Qur'an — twice-stated so that neither the act of worship nor the asking for help is directed toward any created thing. The third movement is petition — verses 6 to 7: ihdinā-ṣ-ṣirāṭa-l-mustaqīm • ṣirāṭa-lladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim • ghayri-l-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-la-ḍ-ḍāllīn (“Guide us to the straight path • the path of those upon whom You have bestowed Your favour • not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who have gone astray”). Ibn Kathīr collects the Companion-identification: the-favoured are the Prophets, the Truthful, the Martyrs, and the Righteous (per An-Nisāʾ 4:69); those who earned anger are those who knew the truth and rejected it (classically identified with the Jews by Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 2954, ḥasan — though the category applies to any community that rejects guidance after knowledge); those who went astray are those who worshipped without knowledge (classically identified with the Christians by the same hadith — again the category applies universally). The hadith is sometimes misread as a blanket condemnation; Ibn Kathīr is careful: the categories are types of failure, and the believer asks Allah every rakʿah to be preserved from both — the failure of rebellion against knowledge and the failure of worship without knowledge. The two together exhaust the ways guidance can go wrong.

Al-Fātiḥah is one of only two surahs explicitly named al-Ruqyah (healing incantation) in the authentic Sunnah. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2276 and 5736 (with parallels in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2201) record the famous Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī narration: a group of Companions on a journey were refused hospitality by a tribe. The tribal chief was then stung by a scorpion, and when the tribe asked the Companions if any among them had a cure, one Companion recited Al-Fātiḥah over the chief, who recovered instantly as if “untied from a bond.” The tribe paid the Companions in sheep. The Companions returned to Madinah uncertain whether to accept the payment, and the Prophet ﷺ asked them, “How did you know Al-Fātiḥah was a ruqyah?” — then said, “You have done the right thing. Divide the sheep and give me a share.” The hadith is ṣaḥīḥ by universal consensus and is cited by Ibn Taymiyyah in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā and Ibn al-Qayyim in Zād al-Maʿād as the primary textual ground for the use of Al-Fātiḥah as healing incantation. The classical fiqh — Ibn Qudāmah in al-Mughnī, al-Nawawī in al-Majmūʿ — permits reciting Al-Fātiḥah over the sick with the intention of invoking Allah's healing. The honesty note matters: the surah is a ruqyah because of the attested miracle in Bukhārī, not because of any inherent magical property of the Arabic letters; the healing is from Allah when the believer draws near to Him through the recitation. Ibn al-Qayyim is explicit in al-Ṭibb al-Nabawī: the surah's efficacy as cure correlates with the certainty and sincerity of the one reciting; it is not a mechanical charm, and the believer who recites it as an idle formula should not expect what the Companion who recited it with conviction received.

The practical fiqh of Al-Fātiḥah is woven through every ṣalāh and makes the surah the most-repeated passage in the Muslim's daily life: seventeen recitations in the five obligatory prayers alone (two in Fajr, four in Ẓuhr, four in ʿAṣr, three in Maghrib, four in ʿIshāʾ), plus every rakʿah of every voluntary prayer, every witr, every eclipse prayer, every ʿīd. A Muslim who prays the five daily obligations recites Al-Fātiḥah no fewer than seventeen times a day — more than six thousand times a year, hundreds of thousands of times over a lifetime. This is why the classical mufassirūn treat the surah as the daily recitation core of the Qur'an: the trio of Al-Ikhlāṣ, Al-Falaq, An-Nās covered in the previous entries is the doctrinal and refuge core — but Al-Fātiḥah is woven through the day itself. Ibn Kathīr closes his commentary on the surah with a reflection that al-Qurṭubī echoes in al-Jāmiʿ: a Muslim who recites Al-Fātiḥah seventeen times a day without reflecting on its content has misunderstood the hadith qudsī. Allah has promised, in Muslim 395, that “My servant shall have what he has asked for” — but the asking must be real. The seven verses are a conversation Allah Himself has written into the believer's daily routine: praise Him first, acknowledge His three domains of lordship, pivot into exclusive worship and exclusive reliance, and petition Him for the straight path with the honest acknowledgment that both knowledge-without-practice and practice-without-knowledge are the failure modes to flee. Everything the believer needs to say to Allah on any given day is contained in these seven verses — which is why Allah, in the ḥadīth qudsī, has made them the pattern of all prayer. Al-Fātiḥah is not an introduction to the Qur'an in the sense of a preface that is read once and set aside; it is the surah the Qur'an is read inside of, the frame within which every other surah of the Qur'an is encountered. This is what the classical mufassirūn mean when they call it Umm al-Kitāb: the Mother of the Book from which the Book is born every time a Muslim stands to pray.
